Situation1: They share their work challenges and personal concerns after noticing their spouse seems worried.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: I sat at the kitchen table, my laptop open, half-listening to my spouse as they stirred dinner. I could see the worry lines on their face, the way their shoulders slumped. I knew I should ask what was wrong, offer comfort, and share my own day. That’s what we promised each other—open communication, no matter how tired or distracted we felt. But my mind kept drifting to the email blinking on my screen. The advocacy group needed my response tonight; a new policy was about to pass that would make it even harder for refugee applicants to access services. I was expected to draft a statement, rally support, and challenge the system before morning. My spouse’s voice broke through my thoughts, soft and uncertain, “Can we talk?” I felt the pull in both directions—toward the person I love, who needed me present, and toward the cause I believe in, which demanded my action. My heart pounded as I tried to decide which expectation I could meet, knowing I couldn’t do both at once.
